# He et al., Cursor adoption, velocity and complexity, Warranting Agent-Built Software Distillation

**Source:** Hao He, Courtney Miller, Shyam Agarwal, Christian Kästner and Bogdan Vasilescu (Carnegie Mellon University), "Speed at the Cost of Quality: How Cursor AI Increases Short-Term Velocity and Long-Term Complexity in Open-Source Projects", arXiv:2511.04427v3, 26 Jan 2026; MSR '26 (ACM), DOI 10.1145/3793302.3793349. Licence: CC BY 4.0. Scope: open.

**Applicability gate (Pass G.0): clear yes.** (1) The source answers practitioner questions this axis asks directly: what will degrade quietly over the next year (warnings, complexity) and what alarm catches it, and whether a run of past successes has become the evidence that a change is safe. (2) Its concepts land naturally in six of the eight phases. (3) Its contrarian position, that an early velocity surge can hide a persistent quality cost which then slows later work, is the axis's second reflex ("it worked first time", success taken as safety) measured at project scale over months.

**Phase mapping.** Primary: Phase 5, Gating deterministically (static-analysis warnings and complexity as the series a gate holds) and Phase 8, Releasing and operating (the month-by-month profile of output, warnings and complexity). Secondary: Phase 7, Warranting the change (early success as weak evidence; the comprehension cost of complexity); Phase 6, Reviewing independently (which new warnings to read first; extra scrutiny for agent code). Supporting: Phase 2, Triaging risk (volume of agent change as a sizing signal) and Phase 3, Locking the tests (coverage that scales with lines added). No rows: Phase 1, Specifying the change (the source says nothing about specifications or acceptance criteria) and Phase 4, Building in the sandbox (it does not study agent permissions, isolation or what an agent can reach).

**Transfer caveat.** The study is observational: a staggered difference-in-differences design over open-source GitHub repositories with at least 10 stars (median 3 contributors, 51 stars) that committed Cursor configuration files, mostly adopting between August 2024 and March 2025. Its estimates are intent-to-treat effects of visible adoption, measured against a state of practice that may already include other AI tools, not against no AI use. It did not study a builder warranting changes for a client, and it did not test any harness gate. Where this distillation carries a finding into the factory's gates, it says the step is its own inference or a harness rule.

## Warranting Agent-Built Software Relevance

This source gives the axis its measured account of what happens to a codebase over months once an agent starts writing much of it. Adopting Cursor brought a large rise in output that lasted about two months, and a rise in static-analysis warnings and code complexity that stayed; the authors' panel models indicate that the accumulated warnings and complexity then slow later output (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, Abstract, p. 1; §4.1, p. 8; §4.2, p. 8) [AE]. For a builder warranting agent-built software, that turns "the last ten changes went fine" into a claim about the short run only: each change can pass its gates while the series those gates should be watching climbs.

The source also tells the harness what to watch and how to read it. Much of the warnings rise tracks codebase growth, so warnings need reading against size, while complexity rose even with velocity dynamics held constant, so it needs its own gate (§4.2, p. 8; §5.1.2, p. 10) [AR]. The authors' practical suggestions (refactoring triggered by quality metrics, test coverage that scales with lines added, extra scrutiny of agent code in review, tools that hold back when debt passes a threshold) are proposals, not tested remedies (§5.2, p. 11) [AR]. Its numbers keep their conditions: open-source repositories, intent-to-treat averages, quality findings that one of three estimators does not reproduce, and a complexity figure the paper prints three ways.

## Key Concepts for Warranting Agent-Built Software

1. <!-- concept: transient-velocity-gain --> **Transient velocity gain.** Averaged over the post-adoption period, lines added rose about 28.6% (p < 0.05) and commits showed no significant change; the only significant gain came in the first two months, with lines added up 281.3% then 48.4% and commits up 55.4% then 14.5% (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §4.1.1, p. 8; Table 2, p. 7) [AE]. In the authors' words: "The only significant development velocity gain is in the first two months post Cursor adoption." (§4.1.1, p. 8) [V]

2. <!-- concept: persistent-quality-decline --> **Persistent rise in warnings and complexity.** Static-analysis warnings rose 30.3% and code complexity 41.6% on average, and both rises persisted beyond the adoption period; duplicate line density showed no significant change (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §4.1.2, p. 8) [AE]. The paper elsewhere prints the complexity rise as 25.1% (§5.1.2) and 25% (§5.2) against 41.64% in Table 2 [AE].

3. <!-- concept: warnings-as-review-effort --> **Warnings as review effort.** The authors call SonarQube's reliability, maintainability and security issues warnings because static analysis can produce false positives, and ask that they be read "as an estimate of the effort required to review potential issues in a project" (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §3.2.1, p. 5) [V]. A rise in warnings is a rise in what someone has to review.

4. <!-- concept: warnings-follow-codebase-growth --> **Warnings follow codebase growth.** Holding other dynamics constant, growth in codebase size absorbed most of the variance in warnings and complexity, and Cursor adoption had no significant effect on warnings (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §4.2, p. 8) [AE]. The authors read this as agent assistants amplifying existing velocity-quality dynamics by producing code faster, possibly adding no more issues than non-adopters moving at the same speed (§5.1.2, p. 10) [AR]. The implication they draw is "that quality assurance needs to scale with AI-era velocity" (§5.1.2, p. 10) [V].

5. <!-- concept: complexity-debt --> **Complexity debt.** Complexity is the exception: with velocity dynamics held constant, adoption still brought "a 9% baseline increase on average compared to projects in similar dynamics but not using Cursor" (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §4.2, p. 8) [V]. The authors take this as strong evidence that Cursor-generated code in their sample is inherently more complex than human-written code (§5.1.2, p. 10) [AR]. They name the result a "complexity debt" in projects that use AI heavily (§5.1.2, p. 10) [V].

6. <!-- concept: debt-slows-velocity --> **Accumulated debt slows later output.** By the panel models, a 100% rise in complexity or in warnings causes a 64.5% or a 50.3% fall in lines added, while adoption brings a 1.84x baseline rise in lines added; the gain would be cancelled by a ∼5x rise in warnings or a ∼3x rise in complexity (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §4.2, p. 8) [AE]. The authors judge that this mechanism alone likely does not explain why the gain vanishes, since rises that large are unlikely (§5.1.1, p. 10) [AR].

7. <!-- concept: technical-debt-accumulation-ratchet --> **The technical debt accumulation ratchet.** The cycle in which a surge in output builds debt that then holds output down (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §1, p. 2; §5.2, p. 11) [AR]. The authors' phrase is "technical debt accumulation ratchet" (§5.2, p. 11) [V]. To get past it they suggest refactoring sprints triggered by code-quality metrics, test coverage requirements that scale with lines added, and engineered Cursor rules that enforce quality standards (§5.2, p. 11) [AR]. These are suggestions; the study does not test them.

8. <!-- concept: comprehension-tax --> **Comprehension tax.** The authors call the complexity rise a "comprehension tax" that persists regardless of functional correctness, and suggest LLMs may generate "structurally valid but semantically opaque code" (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §5.2, p. 11) [V]. Unless a workflow allows fully automated development with no human code review, readability stays important (§5.2, p. 11) [AR].

9. <!-- concept: extra-scrutiny-simpler-implementation --> **Extra scrutiny and the simpler-implementation question.** Until the causes of over-complication are understood and addressed, teams "should treat AI-generated code as requiring extra scrutiny during review" (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §5.2, p. 11) [V], checking whether simpler implementations exist [AR].

10. <!-- concept: new-warning-categories --> **What the new warnings are.** In a descriptive convenience sample of 195,010 warnings, 16 of 20 categories rose after adoption, led by naming conventions, code hygiene (commented-out code, TODOs, unused variables), complexity and style; logic errors (+2.09) and security (+1.98) new warnings per repository per month also rose, which the authors call actual bugs, both detectable and potentially dangerous (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, Appendix D, Tables 8–9, pp. 18–19) [AE]. The first author built the 20-category taxonomy working with Claude Opus 4.5 (Appendix D, p. 18) [AE].

11. <!-- concept: generation-first-tools --> **Generation-first tools and self-limiting output.** The agents of the study period "are generation-first, leaving quality maintenance as an afterthought" (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §5.2, p. 11) [V]. The authors want tools that suggest tests with code, flag unnecessary complexity in real time, recommend refactoring, and, more provocatively, reduce their own suggestion volume when project complexity or debt passes healthy thresholds, forcing consolidation before more generation (§5.2, p. 11) [AR].

12. <!-- concept: intent-to-treat-open-source-estimates --> **Intent-to-treat, open-source, estimator-dependent.** A configuration file "only indicates someone experimented, not that all contributors used it continuously", so the main estimates are intent-to-treat effects (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §3.5.1, p. 7) [V]. One of three estimators gives negative, non-significant quality effects, and the authors write that "the findings around code quality outcomes should be interpreted with appropriate caution" (Appendix B.3, p. 16) [V].

## Questions to Ask During Warranting Agent-Built Software

### Phase 2: Triaging risk

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Size the assurance to the volume | How many lines does this agent change add, across how many files, and has the review and test effort been scaled to that volume rather than to the size of the request? | §1, pp. 1–2; §5.1.2, p. 10 |
| Spot the work agents are said to struggle with | Is the agent working in intricate existing logic, an unfamiliar part of the codebase, or a spec that turns on edge cases, the cases the authors propose (without measuring) as where AI is still limited? | §5.1.1, p. 10 |

### Phase 3: Locking the tests

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Tie test coverage to added code | Is coverage measured on the lines this change adds, or only as a whole-codebase percentage that a large addition can dilute? | §5.2, p. 11 |
| Separate passing from understandable | The tests pass; do we also know whether the change raised complexity, given that the authors' comprehension tax holds regardless of functional correctness? | §5.2, p. 11 |

### Phase 5: Gating deterministically

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Hold the quality series | Does the gate compare this change's static-analysis warnings and complexity with the baseline before it, and stop a rise from passing silently? | §4.1.2, p. 8; §5.2, p. 11 |
| Read warnings against size | Is a rise in warnings read against the growth in code size, since codebase growth absorbed most of their variance? | §4.2, p. 8 |
| Gate complexity on its own | Does complexity have its own threshold, since it rose even with velocity dynamics held constant? | §4.2, p. 8; §5.1.2, p. 10 |
| Set thresholds from the project | Are the thresholds drawn from this project's own series, not from the study's open-source averages? | §3.5.1, p. 7; Appendix B.3, p. 16 |
| Check what a rules file is worth | Is a rules file offered as quality control, and is there a measured change in warnings and complexity to credit it with? | §5.2, p. 11; §4.3, p. 9 |
| Know where to stop adding | Is a module over its warning or complexity threshold still taking new feature work before a consolidating change lands? | §5.2, p. 11 |

### Phase 6: Reviewing independently

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Read the warnings that matter first | Has the reviewer sorted new warnings by category and read logic-error and security warnings before style and naming? | Appendix D, p. 18 |
| Catch leftovers | Does the diff carry commented-out code, TODOs or unused variables, the code-hygiene category that rose sharply? | Appendix D, Table 9, p. 19 |
| Ask the simpler-implementation question | Has the reviewer asked whether a simpler implementation exists, rather than only whether this one works? | §5.2, p. 11 |

### Phase 7: Warranting the change

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Class past success as evidence | Is "the last ten went fine" being read as evidence about quality, when the study's gains were early and transient while warnings and complexity stayed up? | §4.1, p. 8 |
| Name who carries the comprehension cost | If this change raised complexity, who could explain the code without the agent, and is that written down? | §5.2, p. 11 |
| Record the debt | Is any rise in warnings or complexity on the ledger with a paydown plan or a signed waiver? | §5.2, p. 11 |

### Phase 8: Releasing and operating

| Need | Question | Source-tag |
|---|---|---|
| Keep the series | Do we hold a monthly series of output, warnings and complexity from before agents arrived, so a rise is visible against the project's own baseline? | §3.2, p. 5; §4.1, p. 8 |
| Recognise the profile | Did output jump for a month or two after agents were adopted or widened and then fall back, while warnings and complexity stayed up? | §4.1.1–4.1.2, p. 8 |
| Test the counterweights | Have we shown from our own series that the factory's review, tests and gates hold warnings and complexity, rather than assuming they do? | §5.1.3, p. 11 |

## What to Look For

| Signal | Diagnosis | Follow-up |
|---|---|---|
| Output jumps in the first month or two after agents are adopted or widened | The study's average profile: lines added up 281.3% in month one, no significant gain after month two (§4.1.1, p. 8) [AE] | Check whether review and test effort scaled with the volume; start watching warnings and complexity now, not after output falls back |
| Warnings climb in step with code size | Codebase growth absorbs most of the variance in warnings (§4.2, p. 8) [AE] | Read warnings per unit of code as well as in total; hold the gate on the rate as well as the count |
| Complexity climbs faster than code size | Adoption raised complexity with velocity dynamics held constant (§4.2, p. 8) [AE] | Gate complexity on its own; ask the simpler-implementation question in review (§5.2, p. 11) [AR] |
| Output slows a few months after a surge while warnings and complexity stay up | Accumulated warnings and complexity reduce later output, by the panel models (§4.2, p. 8) [AE] | Schedule the paydown before more feature work lands on the same modules |
| New warnings are mostly naming, style and leftover code | The commonest rises in the descriptive sample (Appendix D, p. 18) [AE] | Send leftovers back for cleanup, then check the logic-error and security categories, which also rose (Appendix D, p. 18) [AE] |
| A rules file is cited as the reason quality is fine | The rules are a suggested remedy, untested by the study (§5.2, p. 11) [AR]; quality build-up was stronger, not weaker, in months when configuration files were being changed (§4.3, p. 9) [AE] | Credit only a measured change in the project's warnings and complexity |
| The study's percentages appear in a threshold or a tolerance | Intent-to-treat open-source averages, estimator-dependent for quality, with complexity printed three ways (§3.5.1, p. 7; Appendix B.3, p. 16; §5.1.2, p. 10) [AR] | Derive thresholds from the project's own series |

## When to Use This Reference

- Reach for it when the question is what agent-built code does to a codebase over months, not to one change: it is the corpus's measured account of output, warnings and complexity across adoption.
- Reach for it when designing the quality gates in Phase 5: it says which series to watch (warnings, complexity), how to read them (against code size; complexity on its own) and why a single passing change says little about the series.
- Reach for it in Phase 7 when early success is being offered as the evidence for signing, and in Phase 8 when production signals show output falling back or warnings climbing.
- Reach for another source when the question is felt versus measured speed on one developer's tasks (`becker-metr-ai-developer-productivity-2025`), delivery throughput and instability across organisations (`dora-ai-assisted-swdev-2025`), how strong an agent's tests are (`egashira-testsuitebench-2026`), how to run code review and pull-request gates (`microsoft-code-with-engineering-playbook`), or what a change touches and which security gates that makes mandatory (the standards and threat lists). This source does not cover specifications, sandboxing or security requirements.

## Worked Example

*Scenario (operator-authored).* A two-person studio moved a client's booking web app onto a coding agent six weeks ago. Output has been high: the agent's latest change adds a recurring-bookings feature, about 4,000 lines across 30 files, and every gate passed. The static-analysis report shows complexity in the scheduling module up by about a fifth since adoption, and 14 new warnings on this change, two of them logic-error warnings. The builder wants to sign: the last ten changes shipped clean. The warranty assessor reads the pack and the series, not the diff.

*Applying the source.* The assessor first classes "the last ten went fine" as evidence about the short run. In the study, the output gain was concentrated in the first two months while the rise in warnings and complexity persisted (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §4.1, p. 8) [AE], and the authors' reading of the whole result is this:

> "deliberate process adaptations—those that scale quality assurance with AI-era velocity—are necessary to realize sustained benefits from the use of LLM agent assistants" (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §1, p. 2) [V]

The assessor reads the two series separately, as the panel models suggest (§4.2, p. 8) [AE]. The warnings are checked against how much code the change adds; the complexity rise is not explained by size alone, which is the pattern the authors read as inherent:

> "gives strong evidence that code generated with Cursor in our study sample is inherently more complex than human-written code" (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §5.1.2, p. 10) [V]

The independent reviewer sorts the 14 warnings by category, reads the two logic-error warnings first (logic errors and security rose too in the study's sample, Appendix D, p. 18) [AE], and asks whether the scheduling rules need the nesting the agent wrote, the authors' simpler-implementation question (§5.2, p. 11) [AR]. One logic-error warning is a real off-by-one on the recurrence end date. The reviewer also finds commented-out code and three unused variables, the code-hygiene category that rose sharply in the sample (Appendix D, Table 9, p. 19) [AE].

The builder proposes setting the complexity threshold at *the study's 41%*. The assessor declines: the figure is an intent-to-treat average over open-source repositories, printed as 41.64% in one table and 25% in another passage, and one estimator does not reproduce it (§3.5.1, p. 7; §5.2, p. 11; Appendix B.3, p. 16) [AE]. The threshold comes from the client project's own pre-agent series instead, which is a harness rule, not the source's. The change goes back with three asks: fix the end-date bug with a test for it, remove the leftovers, and simplify the recurrence logic or record a signed waiver with a paydown date. No further feature work goes into the scheduling module until a consolidating change lands, which is this distillation's carrying of the authors' tool proposal into a harness gate (§5.2, p. 11) [AR]. The pack records the complexity rise against the module's own baseline, so the next assessor can see whether the gates are holding.

## Anti-patterns This Reference Helps Avoid

- **Early success as the warranty.** *Signal:* "it's been fine since we switched" carries the sign-off. *Why it fails:* in the study the output gain lasted about two months while warnings and complexity stayed up (§4.1, p. 8) [AE]. *Instead:* read the quality series, not the run of passed changes.
- **One number for all quality.** *Signal:* the gate checks a single quality score. *Why it fails:* warnings tracked codebase growth while complexity rose independently of it (§4.2, p. 8) [AE]. *Instead:* gate warnings against size and complexity on its own.
- **Green as understood.** *Signal:* passing tests are offered as proof the code is fine to keep. *Why it fails:* the authors' comprehension tax persists regardless of functional correctness (§5.2, p. 11) [AR]. *Instead:* ask who can explain the code and whether a simpler implementation exists.
- **Style noise.** *Signal:* new warnings dismissed because most are naming and style. *Why it fails:* logic-error and security warnings rose as well in the sample (Appendix D, p. 18) [AE]. *Instead:* sort by category and read the bug-class warnings first.
- **Rules as a control.** *Signal:* the agent's rules file is offered as the quality control. *Why it fails:* the authors suggest engineered rules as a remedy but do not test them (§5.2, p. 11) [AR]. *Instead:* credit only a measured change in warnings and complexity.
- **Borrowed thresholds.** *Signal:* the study's percentages become the factory's tolerance. *Why it fails:* they are open-source intent-to-treat averages, and the authors ask that the quality findings be read with caution (§3.5.1, p. 7; Appendix B.3, p. 16) [AR]. *Instead:* set thresholds from the project's own series.
- **Assuming the counterweights work.** *Signal:* "we have review and CI, so this doesn't apply to us". *Why it fails:* the authors only suggest that mandatory review, automated testing and dedicated QA might prevent proportional debt accumulation, and leave it to future research (§5.1.3, p. 11) [AR]. *Instead:* show it from the project's series.

## Citation and Source-Integrity Notes

**Borrowed-through gaps.** The prior productivity and quality studies the authors survey, the methods behind their estimators and panel models, the propensity-matching and balance conventions, the literature on technical debt slowing velocity, the qualitative and anecdotal reports they read as aligning with the abandonment explanation, an enterprise study on temporal patterns of tool use, and the reports relaying that training objectives favour passing tests over readability are all cited by the authors and not held in this corpus [BT]. Of the works the paper cites, only Becker et al. is held here (`becker-metr-ai-developer-productivity-2025`).

**Named limits of the source.** The authors ask readers to interpret their results in the context of the setup and its limits (§3.5.1, p. 7) [AR]. Adoption is visible only through committed configuration files, and usage is assumed to continue unless removal is observed, so the estimates are intent-to-treat; Cursor version and model backend are unknown; matching is imperfect; and other AI tools may be in use on both sides, so the comparison is with the state of practice, not with no AI (§3.5.1, p. 7) [AR]. Results may not generalize to other agents, proprietary software or languages beyond JavaScript, TypeScript and Python, and "Results observed may not persist as LLM agent assistants mature and developer workflows adapt" (§3.5.2, p. 7) [V]. The open-source setting is stated as a frame on every finding:

> "Our findings should be interpreted within the specific context of open-source software development" (Source: He et al., Speed at the Cost of Quality, §5.1.3, p. 10) [V]

The quality findings depend on the estimator (Appendix B.3, p. 16) [AR]; Composer and agent-mode users cannot be clearly separated (Appendix C, p. 17) [AR]; the warning-category analysis rests on a convenience sample used descriptively (Appendix D, p. 18) [AR]; and complexity metrics were designed for human-written code, so whether they fairly penalise AI-generated patterns that are mechanically verifiable yet syntactically complex is open (§6, p. 11) [AR]. The excitement-frustration-abandonment cycle is the authors' proposed explanation, not a measured result (§5.1.1, p. 10) [AR]. The study is a snapshot of mid-2024 to mid-2025 tools (§6, p. 11) [AR].

**Evidence-marker continuity.** Results carry `[AE]` as in the deep reference; the authors' readings and proposals (the amplification reading, complexity debt, the ratchet remedies, extra scrutiny, self-limiting tools, the enterprise counterweights) carry `[AR]`; cited prior work carries `[BT]`. Verbatim passages are copied from the deep reference's audited `[V]` quotations (§1, p. 2; §3.2.1, p. 5; §3.5.1, p. 7; §3.5.2, p. 7; §4.1.1, p. 8; §4.2, p. 8; §5.1.2, p. 10; §5.1.3, p. 10; §5.2, p. 11; Appendix B.3, p. 16); none was re-extracted from the tape. Terms the tape broke at line ends (the self-limiting tool proposal, the abandonment cycle) are paraphrased, as in the deep reference. Harness rules (a no-new-warnings gate, thresholds from the project's series, a signed waiver, holding feature work in a module over threshold) are labelled as such or as this distillation's inference. Cross-references in the integration table cite the sibling deep references' own sections.

| Phase | Trigger (what the practitioner notices) | Response (grounded in this source) |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | An agent change adds thousands of lines across many files | Scale the review and test effort to the volume: reviewing large multi-file AI changes differs from reviewing line-by-line completions, and quality assurance needs to scale with AI-era velocity (§1, pp. 1–2; §5.1.2, p. 10) [AR] |
| 2 | The agent is working in intricate existing logic, or the spec turns on edge cases | Require edge-case tests and a reviewer who knows the surrounding code; the authors propose (without measuring) debugging intricate logic, understanding existing codebases and handling edge cases as where AI is still limited (§5.1.1, p. 10) [AR] |
| 3 | An agent change adds code with no tests alongside it, or coverage is checked only as a whole-codebase percentage | Require coverage on the added lines; the authors suggest test coverage requirements that scale with lines added (§5.2, p. 11) [AR] |
| 5 | The diff's static-analysis report shows new warnings or a rise in cognitive complexity | Hold the gate: show the rise against code size and route it to a refactor or a signed waiver (harness rules); accumulated warnings and complexity reduce later output (§4.2, p. 8) [AE] |
| 5 | A module is over the factory's warning or complexity threshold and the agent is adding features to it | Hold feature work there until a consolidating change lands; the authors propose tools that cut their output past healthy thresholds to force consolidation (§5.2, p. 11) [AR]. Carrying this into a gate is this distillation's inference |
| 5 | The agent's rules file is offered as the quality control | Credit the measured change, not the rules: engineered rules are an untested suggestion (§5.2, p. 11) [AR], and quality build-up was stronger in months when configuration was being changed (§4.3, p. 9) [AE] |
| 5 | Someone proposes the study's percentages as the factory's tolerance or threshold | Refuse; derive thresholds from the project's own series. The figures are intent-to-treat open-source averages, estimator-dependent for quality, with complexity printed as 41.64%, 25.1% and 25% (§3.5.1, p. 7; Appendix B.3, p. 16) [AR] |
| 6 | New warnings in an agent diff are dismissed as style noise | Sort by category and read logic-error and security warnings first; those rose too in the descriptive sample (Appendix D, p. 18) [AE] |
| 6 | The diff carries commented-out code, stray TODOs or unused variables | Send it back for cleanup; code hygiene was among the largest rises (Appendix D, Table 9, p. 19) [AE] |
| 7 | A rise in warnings or complexity is in the pack with no paydown and no waiver | Don't sign until it carries a paydown plan or a signed waiver (harness rule); the authors name the debt a ratchet that holds later output down (§5.2, p. 11) [AR] |
| 8 | Output rose for a month or two after agents were adopted or widened, then fell back while warnings and complexity stayed up | Recognise the study's average profile (§4.1, p. 8) [AE]; check whether QA scaled with the output, and pay the debt down before it slows more work (§5.1.2, p. 10; §4.2, p. 8) [AR] |
| 8 | Warnings and complexity climb month after month while every change passed its gates | Check the gates against the project's series, absolute and relative to size; the authors only suggest that review, testing and dedicated QA might prevent proportional debt accumulation (§5.1.3, p. 11) [AR] |
